members.name: Mark Narvais
members.lifeStage: Never married · lives with family/parents · single
members.inWords: "I feel like I have done a good job doing as much as I can for myself mentally and spiritually. Would be nice to get some outside views and guidance with my relationship with my Lord and savior Jesus Christ, as well as more insight on romantic relationships."
members.read: Mature, self-driven, and honestly a bit self-sufficient. His stated worry — "coming into this group & not receiving, or being able to help others grow" — tells you he's oriented toward contributing. He's quietly wrestling with whether he's "living by God's will and not my own."
members.lead: Giving him a role. He'll thrive as a peer-encourager. Gently challenge the self-sufficiency — invite him to receive, not just give. Romantic direction is his felt need.
members.watch: Vacation may pull him from one session (date TBD — confirm with him).

members.name: Jonathon Escalera
members.lifeStage: Never married · lives with roommates · single
members.spiritualState: Inconsistent — some weeks better than others
members.inWords: "I've stagnated. I've definitely not been where I need to be. Not reading my Bible or in prayer. I need someone willing to keep me accountable."
members.read: Self-aware and honest about a plateau. Names a purity struggle plainly (past porn, "can still pop up sometimes when I'm not careful"), and is direct that he needs someone in his corner.
members.lead: Pairing him with an accountability partner early. He's told you exactly what he needs — structure and a check-in rhythm. His candor makes him a good model for the group's honesty culture.
members.watch: Opening up to strangers is hard for him; trip end of August; busy mornings and evenings.

members.name: Steve Lehman
members.church: Just moved to Cheyenne — no church home yet · 10+ years
members.lifeStage: Single dad (shared custody) · lives alone · single
members.mostUrgent: Figuring out how to be single and deal with the heartbreak
members.inWords: "Fiancé just cheated and left me for someone she knew for 3 months. 3.5 years ago my ex-wife cheated. I just moved to Cheyenne and have not met any friends. Not sure how to move forward." He adds he needs "someone to talk to… help building self-esteem and confidence."
members.read: The most raw and at-risk man in the group. Two betrayals, a fresh wound, no church, no friends in a new city, and questioning his faith. His pain is showing up as "I'm not good enough… not sure what I do wrong."
members.lead: Prioritizing connection before content. He needs to be seen and befriended, not fixed. A personal check-in outside group in the first two weeks would matter enormously. Frame identity around belovedness — this is literally the name of the group and his exact need.
members.watch: Doubting faith + isolation = highest pastoral-care priority. Traveling to family in California 7/10–7/14.

members.name: Dane Czarnecko
members.inWords: "I excel at so much and am proud of who I am, but [lust] is a huge part holding me down and I'm ready to win this battle once and for all. It's definitely affected dating."
members.read: Youngest by far (20), confident and capable, but has zeroed in on lust as the one thing holding him back — and he's ready. New to town, wants a band of brothers. High motivation.
members.lead: Meeting his readiness with a concrete purity game plan and an older accountability partner (Jonathon, Dane, and Nate A. share this exact struggle — see analysis). His youth means the older men can pour into him.
members.watch: Cousin's wedding in August (2–3 days) and a South Dakota long weekend — flexible around dates.

members.name: Dustin Michaux
members.lifeStage: Never married · lives alone · relationship status "complicated — I'd like to discuss"
members.commitment: ⚠️ Still deciding if he can commit
members.inWords: "I was living in sin with a girlfriend when I came to Christ. I broke up with her because of her attitude toward my new faith… Recently we've begun to talk again. I've set boundaries but it seems like nothing has changed. It's just complicated." And: "This 10-week program feels like it was built for men like me. I could use some help navigating finding a wife."
members.read: Newer believer navigating a genuinely hard relationship situation in real time — an ex he's reconnecting with, boundaries that aren't holding. Engaged and hungry, broad focus areas.
members.lead: Following up personally to close the commitment gap — his top blocker is simply not knowing the day/time (he asked). Give him the schedule and he's likely in. His live situation is a real-time case study the group can walk with him.
members.watch: ⚠️ Undecided — a schedule answer probably converts him. Asked "what days and times are the meetings?"

members.name: Nathan Green
members.mostUrgent: Loneliness & isolation — "when I interact with others my true self comes out"
members.inWords: "I have been wanting to disciple, but have been doubting how effective I would be. I want to refine my leadership abilities."
members.read: A potential co-laborer. He wants to lead but doubts himself, and carries a quiet ache about "the lack of many experiences others have" and isolation. Growing, engaged, and already looking outward.
members.lead: Handing him small leadership reps — open in prayer, facilitate a breakout. This directly answers his stated desire to grow as a discipler and heals the self-doubt through doing. Alongside Mark, your most likely apprentice-leaders.
members.watch: His isolation is real despite the outward posture — make sure he's genuinely known, not just useful.

members.name: Lloyd Thomas
members.lifeStage: Divorced · lives alone · relationship status "complicated" — "female best friend I'd love to date"
members.commitment: ⚠️ Still deciding if he can commit
members.inWords: "Need a men's group." On concerns: "Not sure I have many." On timing: "I have no idea when this starts."
members.read: The most tentative applicant — short answers, "no idea now," undecided. The oldest man, divorced, walking with a hard-to-name longing (a best friend he wants to date). His guard is up, or he's simply weary.
members.lead: Low-pressure personal outreach. Give him the concrete schedule (his one clear blocker) and a warm, specific invitation. Don't over-program him early; let brotherhood do the work. He may open up slowly.
members.watch: ⚠️ Undecided + low engagement in the form = the applicant most likely to no-show without a personal nudge. Doesn't know start date.

members.name: Nate Applehans
members.lifeStage: Never married · lives with roommates · single
members.inWords: "I want to grow in my faith and have a family. I feel like I am behind in starting a family. I wish to break habits and form new ones."
members.read: Young (25) but carrying a "behind on life" pressure about marriage and family. Broad set of focus areas — identity, purity, dating, shame, disciplines — which reads as a man who wants a full reset and new patterns. No church home ("many different churches") is worth gently exploring.
members.lead: Naming the "break habits, form new ones" desire as a whole-group goal — he'll feel at home. Connect the family longing to identity work so the timeline pressure eases. Pairs naturally with Dane and Jonathon on purity.
members.watch: Tax accountant — overtime in August/September (extension season) may hit attendance in the back half.

analysis.pattern: All 8 men are unmarried — 6 never married, 1 divorced, 1 single dad. Every one of them is navigating singleness, dating, or relationships. This is not a group with a relationship sub-theme; relationships are the water everyone is swimming in. Whatever else you plan, dating/identity/purity as a single man is the through-line.

pillars.title: Brotherhood / belonging (the #1 draw)
pillars.body: "Brotherhood — real community" was the single most-chosen primary driver (5 of 8: Steve, Dane, Dustin, Lloyd, Nate A). Several are new to Cheyenne or isolated (Steve and Dane just moved; Nathan G, Lloyd, and Steve all live alone and named loneliness). The group itself is the medicine. Protect unstructured connection time. Don't over-teach at the expense of relationship — for at least half these men, being known is the point.

pillars.title: Dating, singleness & purity (the shared life-stage)
pillars.body: Six named dating; four named purity directly, and three men are wrestling with it right now — Jonathon, Dane, and Nate A. are a natural purity accountability triad (all name lust/porn, all want new habits). Meanwhile Dustin, Lloyd, and Steve are each in a specific, live relational situation (a reconnecting ex, an unrequited best friend, fresh betrayal). Plan to cover both the discipline side (purity, habits) and the wisdom side (dating as a believer, heartbreak, boundaries).

pillars.title: Spiritual disciplines & identity (the engine)
pillars.body: Six named disciplines/growth, and four describe their walk as "inconsistent" (Jonathon, Dane, Lloyd, Nate A) with one more "doubting" (Steve). This group is spiritually hungry but stalled — the felt need is consistency and accountability, not more information. Marry this to identity (3 named it): the group is called The Crown Season, and Steve, Nathan G, and Nate A are each fighting a "not good enough / behind / true self hidden" narrative. Grounding identity in belovedness is the spine that holds dating, purity, and shame together.

emphasis: ~3 weeks — Identity & belovedness (who you are in Christ; shame; "not enough"). Front-load this — it disarms Steve's, Nathan's, and Nate A's core wound and sets the frame.
~3 weeks — Dating, singleness & purity (as a single Christian man; heartbreak; boundaries; the lust battle). The largest shared felt-need.
~2 weeks — Spiritual disciplines & consistency (prayer, Word, habits — for the four "inconsistent" men). Build the accountability structure here.
~1 week — Calling, work & money (Mark and Jonathon's financial concern; Dustin/Lloyd's purpose).
~1 week — Brotherhood / commissioning (send-off; keep the community going past week 10).
Throughout: consistent accountability pairings and real relationship time every session.

actionItems: Two men are undecided — Dustin and Lloyd. Both listed the same_ blocker: they don't know the meeting day/time. A single text with the schedule likely converts both. Dustin literally asked, "what days and times are the meetings?"
Publish the schedule to everyone. Multiple men asked when it starts (Dustin, Lloyd) — communicate dates ASAP.

notes: This session is the foundation for everything. If men leave Week 1 with a crack in the "singleness means unchosen" narrative, the rest of the curriculum has room to work.

Be prepared for father wounds to surface. "Abba Father" is complicated for men whose fathers were absent or cold. Acknowledge it: "For some of you the word father doesn't carry warmth — that's real. We'll go deeper into that in Week 3."
The "I am the beloved" exercise will feel embarrassing to many men. Normalize that: "It feels awkward because most of us have never been told to say it. Do it anyway."
Share your own honest answer to the opening question. Don't skip this — if the leader struggles to answer "who are you" without his roles, that vulnerability opens the room.
The Impostor concept hits men two ways: some recognize themselves immediately and feel exposed; others deflect with humor. Both are the Impostor at work. Give room for both.
Make it concrete: "The reason your prayer life feels hollow might be because the Impostor is praying — performing for an audience rather than actually talking to God."
Accountability partners should be assigned tonight. Take time at the end to physically pair men off, exchange numbers, and agree on a check-in question for the week.
This is the most emotionally loaded session of the series for many men. Pray specifically before this one.
Do not push men to "resolve" their father wounds in 90 minutes. The goal is naming and turning, not healing. Progress in this area is slow and non-linear.
Watch for the man who intellectualizes — "I've processed this already" — or the man who goes completely quiet. Both deserve a private follow-up this week.
If someone discloses abuse, do not handle it in the group. Thank him for his honesty and connect him privately with a pastor or counselor.
Leader: share your own father story. If you don't, the room won't. This session requires the most personal honesty from the leader of any week in this series.
Prepare spiritually before this session more than any other. Pray for each man by name.
Watch for the man who goes very quiet. Follow up with him individually this week.

If anyone discloses something requiring professional support (compulsive behavior significantly affecting his life, illegal content), thank him for his honesty and connect him with a pastor or counselor privately.
End the session pointing clearly to grace: there is no sin here beyond the reach of God. Peter denied Jesus three times and was given the keys to the Kingdom.
By Week 5, the room has four sessions of history. Acknowledge that: "We've been at this for a month. Take stock of what's happened in this room."

Some men will be reluctant to name loneliness — it feels like a weakness. Be the first to name your own. "I have been lonely in ways I didn't tell anyone about for years." That kind of leader honesty unlocks the room.
The reach-out challenge is powerful precisely because it's done together. Men who do it alone often don't follow through. The social accountability of doing it in the room means it actually happens.

This week is a bridge week. The content connects the identity work (Weeks 1–4) to the brotherhood and relationship work (Week 6). Name that explicitly: "We've been working on who you are. Now we're starting to work on who you're doing this with."
The "pursuing from emptiness" concept often lands with unexpected weight. Men recognize themselves quickly. Give room for that without rushing to solutions.
Some men will be nursing relational wounds — recent rejection, a broken relationship. Don't minimize it. The call to pursue from fullness is not dismissive of real grief. It is the path through it.
Name what this group itself is building: "What we're trying to build here is exactly what this session is about — men who will tell each other the truth and not let each other drift."

The stewardship section can feel convicting to men who have been drifting. Be careful not to shame — the goal is vision, not guilt. "Here is what is possible" lands better than "here is what you have been wasting."

Be sensitive to men who are genuinely struggling financially. The "be generous now" message lands differently for someone carrying significant debt or struggling to make rent. Acknowledge that context explicitly.

This session requires the most leader courage. Men are comfortable talking about sexual sin. They are far less comfortable talking about anger, entitlement, and passive control — which are often more visible to everyone around them than to themselves.

Lead with your own shadow. Name a specific pattern — not a vague tendency. "I go cold. I get quiet and then wonder why no one knows what's wrong." That level of specificity gives men permission to be equally specific.

The connection to the belovedness theme (Weeks 1–3) is critical. Don't let this week feel like a character improvement lecture. It is another angle on the same root question: what happens when a man doesn't yet believe he is loved?
Watch for the man who deflects with humor. Anger is the topic men are most practiced at avoiding. Don't let the room stay light.
Some man in this room has been carrying something for years that he believes disqualifies him. Tonight is the night to offer him Peter's story — not as a sermon point, but as a real thing.
Begin the letter prompt tonight so it has one week to breathe before the sealing ceremony in Week 10.
Ask the room what comes next. Have an answer ready before you walk in: another series, monthly dinners, accountability pairs that keep meeting, an invitation to multiply into a new group.
This is the most important night logistically. Have paper and envelopes ready before anyone arrives. Have the calendar reminder for 12 months out set before the session ends.
Give the letter exercise its full 15 minutes. Silence in a room of men doing something real is rare and sacred. Don't rush it.
After the closing prayer, don't clean up immediately. Stay. Let conversations happen. Some of the most important moments of the whole series happen in the parking lot on the last night.
Follow through on mailing the letters in 12 months. It communicates: you were thought about long after this room closed. That is not a small thing.

Have a clear answer for "what's next?" Don't let the group dissolve into nothing. Options: continue with a new series, monthly dinners, accountability pairs that keep meeting, or an invitation to multiply into a new group. Momentum dies without structure.
